utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-16-T, the Prosecutor versus Zoran Kupreskic, Mirjan Kupreskic, Vlatko Kupreskic, Drago Josipovic, Dragan Papic, and Vladimir Santic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning. I see the witness is already there, Mr. Kupreskic, I imagine. Mr. Kupreskic, could you please stand and make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: I can't find here the English translation. I don't have any. I didn't see it. Okay. Thank you. Good morning, Your Honours. I would just like at the outset, before the examination-in-chief, to say that witness Ivica Kupreskic has been proposed as a witness for Vlatko Kupreskic, and that he is on his list of witnesses as well, so that my colleagues, Mr. Par and Mr. Krajina, will also be performing part of the cross-examination -- I'm sorry, examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter apologises.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: IVICA KUPRESKIC

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. Kupreskic, good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Would you introduce yourself to the Court, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Ivica Kupreskic. I was born on the 12th of April, 1955, in Pirici, Vitez. I am at present residing in Petar Svacic Street in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Where was your house in 1992 when you lived in Pirici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My house in 1992 when I lived in Pirici was located precisely in Pirici.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Could you take a look at the aerial photograph of Ahmici and point out where your house is located.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is my house (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Very well. Tell us, please, the houses located around your own house, who do they belong to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is Zoran Kupreskic's house. This is Vlatko Kupreskic's warehouse, that is Vlatko Kupreskic's house. This is the house belonging to Mirjan's father, Anto Kupreskic. This is my brother's house, Josip Kupreskic. This other house here belongs to my brother, Branko Kupreskic, and that is where my father Ivica Kupreskic's house is. Do you want me to go on?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You said -- very well, you said Josip and Branko. Which other houses were there in that part? There were some old houses there, apart from these, were there not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. In that part, on the upper side, upwards from our own houses, there was Enver Sehic's house, there was the house of Alaman Ahmic, there was the house of Zulejha Ahmic and Sakib Ahmic's house, his son's house, Sukrija Ahmic, Krdzalic's house, Meho Hrustanovic's house. Then there was the house belonging to Redzib Ahmic, further on, Suad Ahmic as well. Is that enough?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Would you please tell the Court the people that you enumerated, that they were around the Kupreskic houses, were they all Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were all Muslims on the section of the road from the main road running from Vitez to Busovaca, which means on the right-hand side going towards the warehouse. Towards the warehouse, as I say, here we had our neighbours living, our Muslim neighbours. In this -- on this part of the road, towards upper Pirici, they were also Muslims, except the house belonging to Vlatko Kupreskic, which lies in that part, and his warehouse as well, Zoran Kupreskic's house and Mirjan's father's house, Anto Kupreskic, and his son Mirjan. All the other houses belonged to Muslims. They were all Muslim neighbours on the right-hand side. Looking at it from the road, that is to say on the right-hand side from the main road going up towards Gornji or Upper Pirici.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And when you used the road to Gornji Ahmici, Upper Ahmici, were the Muslim houses on the right-hand side as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were all our Muslim neighbours. That is to say in this whole section here, they were our Muslim neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You said that around your own house, next to your own house was Zoran Kupreskic's house, Branko's and Josip Kupreskic's house -- just a moment, please. Tell us your relationships, family relationships, with all these individuals. How are you related?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zoran, I, Mirjan, and Vlatko are the children of three brothers, which means we're cousins.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Branko and Josip Kupreskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Branko and Josip Kupreskic are my brothers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. You may resume your seat. You pointed out to us on the map that around you there were all Muslims, so they were Muslim houses around you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What relationships did you have with your Muslim neighbours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you this: We always had exceptionally good relations, and I know that never in my life did I have any problems. I even had -- my best men were Muslims, and godfathers and so on, and one of them was godfather to my eldest son; Varupa Vahid, his name was. My second son, Josip, who was born in 1980, 23. (redacted) And at the same time, we were also in this kind of family, godfatherly relationship with (redacted), and I married Gordana Vidovic. I was best man to him and his wife in his last marriage, because he had several marriages before that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Suad Ahmic, you said you were best man and godfather with Redzib Ahmic as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, with Redzib Ahmic as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Tell me, in 1992, where were your brothers, Branko Kupreskic and Josip Kupreskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My brother Branko, a long time ago, that is to say 18 years ago, went to work abroad. To be more exact, he went to Deutschland, Germany. He has a restaurant there. As I say, he has a restaurant in the town of Herne. And also, in 1992 my brother Josip went there, too. He went to work with our other brother in the kitchen.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: That was in 1992, do you know what month it was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that it was January 1992 when Josip went to work for him.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did Josip's family go with him, and Branko's family, did they go with him to Germany?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Branko's family was already in Germany. However, Josip's family -- that is to say his children, as he had divorced his first wife, and from that marriage he had two children -- and my three children, my wife, and myself, we went on the trip to Germany on the 30th of March. The 30th of March, 1992, we set out for Germany. Because of the situation which already at that time had taken place in the area of Yugoslavia at that time, what had already happened was the village of Ravno and Derventa, and quite simply I tried to do the best I could for my family, to look after them. And because it was safe at my brother's place in Germany, we decided to go to Germany.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: When you say that the village of Ravno and Derventa occurred, what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you this way: The first Croatian village was attacked, and it was the village of Ravno.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Who attacked it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was attacked by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And what about Derventa?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Derventa was also attacked by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: That means in fact that you wanted to get away from the Serbian aggression, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did, from the Serbian aggression.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So you went to Germany?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And who went with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My wife, Ankica, went with me, as well as my three sons, Dragan, Josip, and Ivica. And then my brother Josip's two children, Goran and Ivana, they also went.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You said that that was in March, at the end of March 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly on the 30th of March, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you work in Germany? What happened there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I went to Germany to take my family there and to try to do some work there, if that was possible. My brother, Branko, as soon as I arrived, found me a job. And as I am a caterer by profession, I worked for a time at his restaurant, and I was a waiter there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: How long were you in Germany?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About two and a half months.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, what happened was that my father informed me that I should return from Germany because there were problems in the area, and quite simply, the Croats wanted to take away the property that I had in that region.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did that mean that they treated you as a deserter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, precisely that. They treated me as a deserter. And quite simply I had to make that next move and return home so as to retain my property.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Was that an official or unofficial threat? Was it just rumoured or did an official call-up come for you? Were you officially asked to report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No official invitation came. However, through the village, in that part, it was rumoured. That was the rumour. That was what people said. As my father was close to all these events, he heard about this, and he told me and told me to return urgently.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: When did you go back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went back from Germany in the middle of June.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Where did your family stay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My family stayed in the town of Essen in my brother's apartment there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Your wife and children stayed there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, my wife and my children stayed in that apartment.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You went back in, as you said, the middle of June 1992; did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you take with you any kind of humanitarian aid?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went back because, with a relative of mine who lived in Feldberg, I had organised a humanitarian aid package, and for that reason, to come to Vitez -- to make it easier to come back to my own people in Vitez. We took this humanitarian aid, it was in the form of medicaments, and we used two vehicles, two ambulances, for the Novi Travnik first aid department. This can be seen from the title page of the Bild Zeitung from Feldberg, the daily newspaper. I don't know exactly what date that article came out.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: I should now like to call upon the usher to hand this page from the newspaper and to show it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D99/2.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I apologise, but the witness brought this document with him when he came here today. We haven't had time to translate it, but we shall be handing in a translation in due course.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: On the first page, on this picture, who do we have there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You can see, first of all, myself standing next to the vehicle on the left-hand side, my relative Vlado Sucic who has his restaurant in Feldberg. This next man, the gentleman on the right-hand side of the Opel Granada vehicle, he's a German, and also on the left-hand side next to the kombi van carrying the medicaments, on the left-hand side, the first is myself. Then you have Vlado Sucic, a relative of mine, and the other German gentleman.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: The title is "Six Men on the Road to War"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: The date the paper was issued, can you read it out to us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the 13th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: How did you return?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we returned -- took a long road from Germany.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: I wanted to know which vehicle. I misspoke. Which vehicle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I was driving the Opel Granada vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So it is the vehicle that was part of the humanitarian aid?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was part of this humanitarian shipment which was intended for the first aid department in Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Which vehicle did you use to go to Germany?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went to Germany with a Mercedes 240D, and I took my wife and children in that car. I left the car in Germany so that my wife could have it at her disposal, so she could use it while she was there in Germany.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: This humanitarian aid, you were taking to Novi Travnik; is that right? Where else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Vitez. Part of the medicaments were left in Novi Travnik and part of the medicines were left in Vitez, and this was personally taken over by a doctor who was a dentist, Dr. Bruno Buzuk. Also present when this aid was being handed over was the mayor, the then mayor who was Mr. Ivica Santic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: In Novi Travnik, who did you hand the medicines over to, the first aid department or the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Novi Travnik, we handed this over to Dr. Dzambas, and it was the first aid station in Novi Travnik, not the hospital there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What kind of situation did you encounter in Ahmici when you returned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I returned from Germany, everything was new to me, to put it simply. In the meantime, joint patrols had been established because, at that moment, things were done jointly. I don't know how these were organised. However, when I arrived, I joined the village patrols at once, the village guard.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So you joined the village guard.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You said they were joint guards at that time, Muslim and Croatian.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Does that mean you patrolled together?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we patrolled together. Since at our school in Ahmici, there was a radio transmitter, someone was on duty there all night.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Who maintained this transmitter in the school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All I know is that Mr. Sefik Pezer was on duty there, but there were others as well. I can't say now who they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: But whose was this transmitter? Who was Sefik Pezer? Did any Croats keep duty there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not at the transmitter. We did have a joint village guard, but it happened at that time that the Muslims who manned the radio transmitter were trained to use it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So they used the transmitter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What happened? Since you mentioned the school and the radio transmitter, what happened next?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we had the joint village guards on my return for maybe less than a month. Then one of our patrols consisting of two men came to take over the shift, and they were denied entry into the school, into the classroom where the radio transmitter was. They were told that we could no longer keep watch together.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Were other people allowed to enter the school or the classroom where the radio transmitter was, other members of the village guards, Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No one was allowed from that moment into the school, especially the room where the radio transmitter was.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: When you say that a two-man patrol was denied entry, do you know who the people were who were denied entry?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That evening, the men on patrol were Mr. Mirko Vidovic and Mirjan Kupreskic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: After that, it was no longer permitted for Croats to enter that classroom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Croats were not allowed to enter the classroom at all after that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: When you said that the village guards separated then, what does that mean? Did you continue keeping guard and where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it did mean that, because the very idea of no longer being allowed to keep guard together led us to organise ourselves at our own houses. Since we were very close neighbours, we felt we had to keep watch for our personal security and for the security of our houses and our property. However, since there were very few of us, because there were only a few Croatian houses there, we were joined by the people from Pudzine Kuce which is the first hamlet nearby, and then we would patrol around our houses. I was away very often, and so was Vlatko. Mirjan played very often. He was often obliged to go and play. So most of the time, I simply observed what was going on from my balcony because I have quite a good view in the direction of the school.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Were there any periods when no watch was kept at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There were such periods when there was simply no one around. Everyone had something else to do. So one of us would walk around on his own and then go home to bed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Were there any incidents where you had to intervene or was everything quiet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there were no incidents. The situation was really quiet, regardless of everything.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: At that time, did you see the Muslims keeping guard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They kept watch all the time, especially near the radio transmitter, which was located in the school in the left-hand classroom and looking from the direction of my house. I had a very good view of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Were the guards kept every day and every night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they kept watch day and night by the radio transmitter.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did the Croats have a radio transmitter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, the Croats did not have a radio transmitter.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Court, just before the first conflict on the 19th of October, 1992, where were you, and did you have any hints that something might happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, on the 19th of October, I was away. In the evening at around 5.00 p.m., I was on my way back, and I arrived from the direction of Split, along the Vitez-Busovaca road. When I turned off into my village, there was a roadblock that had been set up about ten metres away from the junction with the main Vitez-Busovaca road. The roadblock was made of wooden objects, and on the right-hand side, there were wooden blocks. There were trestles and wooden blocks, blocks of wood.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So these are building materials?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They had set up next to the garage a little shed where they could take shelter from the rain if it rained.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So the roadblock was on the road leading to Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Was there anything else at that roadblock? Did you notice anything else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I noticed two anti-tank mines which had been set up on the road itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Were there any men there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were. I was stopped by my best man, Suad Ahmic. He was accompanied by Pezer Sezahija, Pezer Ibrisim. Then there was Zahid Ahmic. As far as I know at that time, he was the commander. He was wearing a military uniform. There were about ten other people whom I didn't know and who were manning the roadblock.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Were these people armed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were armed. Suad Ahmic was wearing a uniform, an SPS uniform, since he was a guard at the SPS at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: The people you recognised from the village, were they armed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What happened at the roadblock?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Suad stopped me and asked me, "Where are you coming from now?" I said, "I'm coming home from a trip." Then I said, "What's this? Are there any problems?" He told me, "No, there are no problems. This is just for the security of the village." He told me that there were no problems and that I could pass through in safety and reach my house.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Do you know that there was another roadblock at that time near the cemetery?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time, I did not know anything about it, since I was coming home from a journey; however, I found out the following morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What did you do then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They took away one anti-tank mine and one wooden trestle so that I could pass through. I went to my house. However, on the way to my house, in front of Zoran Kupreskic's house, I saw Zoran, and he was stripping the bark off a piece of wood. So I stopped there and I asked him, "Zoran, do you know, by any chance, what's going on and why this roadblock has been set up?" He answered, "No, I don't know anything," and he continued stripping the bark off the log. I continued on my way to my house. I took the telephone and I rang up Mr. Nenad Santic to see whether he might know something about the roadblock. He told me that he had no idea why it was there, that he really knew nothing about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Why did you ring up Nenad Santic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I rang up Nenad Santic, first of all, because he was one of the founders of the local HDZ from the very beginning, and he had the most information, but also because we have best man and godfather connections four times over.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So he said he knew nothing. What did you do then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I accepted this. I thought if they knew anything, then they would probably address us. They would tell us and warn us of any problems. However, as the night advanced, since my family was in Germany and I was in the house on my own and I was a bit worried about the fact that a roadblock had been set up, I simply went out, out onto the balcony by myself. As I said, I have a rather good view of that part of the village. I sat on my balcony, simply watching, listening to the sounds, paying attention to what was happening around me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did anything unusual occur?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At about 1.00 a.m., which means it was already the 20th, I heard the rattle of weapons and the murmur of human voices arriving from the direction of Redzib Ahmic's house, beside Vlatko Kupreskic's house. In front of Vlatko Kupreskic's warehouse, there was a light on in front of the warehouse, and I saw that it was a column of soldiers with equipment, with arms, and they went to the school. When they arrived at the school, they went into the right-hand classroom, looking from the direction of my house. That's not the one where the radio transmitter was. Then the light went on in the classroom itself, and I saw the silhouettes of the men. I couldn't recognise them at that time because this was about 400 metres away from my house.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: How did you recognise that these people were soldiers? What did you see that they had?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they went past the warehouse, which is about 80 metres away from my house. They passed in front of that light, and I saw that they were fairly well-armed individuals wearing uniforms. There were about 30 to 40 of them in that group.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Were you able to conclude where they were coming from? You said that you saw them coming by Redzib's house.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that particular moment, I did not know where they were coming from. However, in a day or two, we received information that they had come as reinforcements from the neighbouring villages of Vrhovine, Poculica, and Preocica.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What happened next? You said that you saw them in the classroom in the school.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They entered the school building, and probably at that particular moment, that army was sort of deployed from the direction of the cemetery, the mosque, Vlatko Kupreskic's warehouse, beside Zoran Kupreskic's house --

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Just a minute. Tell me, how do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I was on the balcony, and Zoran's house isn't further off than, say, 15 or 20 metres at the most from my own house. Behind Zoran's house, in the garden of Sakib Ahmic, there were two or three old battered cars. There were some branches that had been cut from the forest, and they were rotten already, they had rotted, and when you get close to Zoran's house, two or three, not more, I heard men talking as they drew close to his house, and you could hear the breaking of branches and twigs as they stepped on them. They had, in fact, gone past those discarded vehicles and probably did not know the terrain very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So you heard people going past Zoran's house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I went into the house. I took up the telephone and called Zoran. I asked him, I said, "Zoran, what are you doing now?" He said, "I'm sleeping." I said to him, "Well, you can go on sleeping, but don't forget that there are two or three men underneath the window of your house."

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what time all this took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was about 2.30, between 2.30 and 3.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What happened next? Did Zoran wake up and --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zoran got ready and went out of his house. He took the road towards his father's house, and then from the upper part of my own house, he came to my balcony there or terrace. He went into my house, and when I told him everything that was going on, he went into my house, took up the telephone, and he woke up his brother Mirjan Kupreskic. Shortly after that, Mirjan came onto my terrace, and we stayed there until morning. In the morning, at about 5.00 a.m., when you could generally hear the morning prayer coming from the mosque, we heard before that a long burst of gunfire. After that, from the mosque, we heard some unusual music, the kind of music we had never heard until then. It did not last long, perhaps some 10 seconds, and then you could hear a voice from the mosque, from the loudspeaker there, and it said, "Croats surrender. This is the holy Jihad war." After that, we heard one detonation and then another one. I laid down on the floor of my terrace. I simply did not know what was going on. I thought I had been hit myself. After that, there was another burst of gunfire, it was misty, and then everything was quiet.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you hear what was hit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You could only hear how pieces of the roof from the mosque fell off, and when it became light, we saw that the mosque had, in fact, been hit at the very top of the minaret.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you stay on the terrace?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We stayed on the terrace. We did not know what was going on. We tried to telephone and to learn of any of the details; however, everything was quiet. There was not a single bullet fired after that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you see any Muslim soldiers around your house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that moment, we did not see anybody yet. It became light, but it was misty. It was daybreak, but misty. And sometime around 6.00, perhaps it was a little after 6.00, in front of my house, my neighbour turned up, Enver Sehic. And I respected him highly as a neighbour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Tell us, so Enver Sehic came, and what happened to Enver Sehic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Enver Sehic came to my house and asked me about Zoran and Mirjan, who were on my terrace. I called to them, and allegedly -- he said he had come for them to go with him to bring in wood, firewood, for his house, in view of the fact that he was such a good neighbour. He had helped previously, he had helped Zoran and Mirjan bring in firewood for their own house. So he was an exceptionally good man. I would often sit with him. I told him that I would have to do some gardening around my house, to cut down some grass and so on, and in the morning when I woke up. And once when I woke up on one particular morning, he had already cut the grass, half the grass around my house.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And did you ask Enver Sehic what was happening and whether he knew what was going on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Enver asked me. He said, "Neighbour, what's all this going on? I heard two detonations." And I said that I didn't know what was happening myself, that I had tried to contact people and to see what was in fact happening, but that I had not been successful. I said to him, "I really don't know." As his wife was working in Austria at the time, he had three small children, and he told me, he said, "Neighbour, I'm going to collect my children, and I'm going to go to my house, to Zenica, across the hill," because I think his native village was Dvinjo (phoen), near Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Why did he want to leave? Did he tell you why he was leaving, why he had decided to go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, he said that something smelt wrong, and that means that he probably supposed that there could be some problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What happened next? Could you hear gunfire again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, serious gunfire. And it began sometime about 6.30 in the morning, so almost one and a half hours after the detonations. And that was, in my view, something that we had never experienced, this kind of war, this kind of terrible gunfire and shooting. And afterwards they began shooting with heavy weapons as well, Brownings or some other types of weapons like that. I don't really know much about them. But for the most part, I had never experienced anything like it before, nor did I know where to go to, where to escape, where to flee. I just felt completely lost.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And where was the shooting? Was it concentrated in one part or was it distributed in several locations in the village? Were you able to assess this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The shooting, most of the shooting took place in the area of what we call Donja or Lower Ahmici, around the cemetery there, around the mosque, and up to Vlatko Kupreskic's warehouse. There were bullets flying past, quite simply, they would fly past our own houses, up in our section.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you see any soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were -- yes, there were soldiers. I saw people in front of the warehouse belonging to Vlatko Kupreskic. There was a sort of big hill, mound, which isn't there any more, and the army, that army, and I have in mind the Muslim army, had reached that mound, and it is almost parallel to my own house, running from the mosque. That's where I noticed that with the machine guns, that Budo had a machine gun, I don't know his surname, but his house is right (redacted) 23. (redacted) It's a small weekend cottage, in fact, and he came to live in our village when he built that cottage, and Hajrudin Pezer who was from Gornji or Upper Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you see them shooting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't see them shooting in the direction of Pudzine Kuce, Zume, from that hill.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you say -- I'm sorry, did you say that you had seen them, or hadn't seen them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw them. I did see them, as it is some 80 metres from my house.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You said, therefore, that they were two individuals whom you recognised?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I recognised those two individuals.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you see any soldiers, other soldiers, up there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I saw five soldiers. They ran across from Mirko Kupreskic's house towards -- no, Mirka Vidovic's house, I'm sorry. They ran from Mirko Vidovic's house towards the house of Rudo Vidovic. That house is situated further towards Zume. There were five of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you recognise them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not. I did not. From the -- they were located on the lower side of Mirko Vidovic's house.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Were you able to assess -- you did not recognise them, you say, but were you able to assess whether they were Muslim soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, later on I learnt that they were, in fact, Muslim soldiers because they had stormed the warehouse in which Gordana Vidovic and her mother were, Milka Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: They went into the warehouse? Why did they do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I didn't talk to them personally.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did they do anything to the women you mentioned, Gordana Vidovic and Milka Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they didn't. Nothing. And this is something that Mrs. Gordana Vidovic will be able to explain to you better, because she was on the spot.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Where were Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic at that particular moment when the shooting began?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When the shooting began, they had started to evacuate their families. Zdravko Vrebac came, as did Dragan Vidovic, nicknamed Dragance, and Milutin Vidovic turned up. They helped Zoran and Mirjan, as Mirjan had small children as well, and so did Zoran, they came to help to take the children away, and wives, of course. I asked whether they needed my help, and they said no. But I went down to the valley with them, depression with them, which leads towards Pudzine Kuce.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So you followed them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, but I stayed in the valley.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you see where Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic's families went?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They went in the direction of Pudzine Kuce, and I later learned from them that they had been accommodated in the shelter at Jozo Vrebac's house, or his son-in-law's house; I think his name is Trajanovski.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: How long did the women and children of Mirjan and Zoran Kupreskic stay away from their house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, as I heard from them, they soon moved their families to the house of their sister, Zorica, who lives perhaps some 500 metres further away from that shelter, the Trajanovski shelter, in the direction of Santici. I think that their families returned to their homes on the fourth day, when the Muslims also started returning to their homes, because there was already some feeling of security. And we thought, well, if they were coming back, then our families can come back too.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You said that you went to Odolina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: The valley, sorry. Where is this valley?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This valley is behind my father's house, beneath my father's hayloft, behind Stipan Vidovic's wood, on the path leading towards Niko Sakic's house and on to Pudzine Kuce.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Why did you go there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I went there because at that moment, I had already seen that the soldiers had run by the Vidovics's house, which is further along the road to Pudzine Kuce, and that our houses were behind them now. And, of course, I was afraid.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you find anyone in the valley when you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I found Niko Sakic, Mirko Sakic, and I think it was -- I think Dragan Samija was there, too, already in the valley at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And who were these people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These were neighbours who live behind our houses. In other words, they live right behind the wood where the path leads toward Pudzine Kuce.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You mentioned Zdravko Vrebac arriving?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Milutin Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. And Milutin Vidovic, Zdravko Vrebac, and Dragan Vidovic, nicknamed Dragance. He was Nikica's son. There is another Dragan Vidovic who is the son of Stipan.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether the people you saw and the people you found in this depression were armed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, at that moment, I saw only Mirko Sakic with a hunting rifle, and Zdravko Vrebac who had a rifle at that time. Nobody else was armed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: These persons who were armed, did they use their weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, they were hiding. They didn't know what was going on, as I didn't know either.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you have any weapons at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't have any weapons then.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they had no weapons then.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you see any other soldiers, soldiers on the Croatian side, taking part in the conflict that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In fact, there were no soldiers, but we heard horrific gunfire later on. I think that the detonations were really serious. But we were completely lost. We had found this depression to hide in, and from time to time -- we were curious, so we would crawl underneath the hayloft, because the path leading to the depression, which was used only to grow grass, there was a pathway at the side of the hill, and we would crawl there because we were curious. We wanted to see what was going on. My aunt, who is now 75 years old, didn't want to leave the house, so she cooked some lunch for us. So we all had lunch underneath the hayloft. I remember that well. And the gunfire was very, very strong in that part, and it moved more and more in the direction of Gornji or Upper Ahmici. By the sound, we could see that it was moving in the direction of Gornji Ahmici on that day. And this went on until about 4 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So not only did you hear gunfire around the road, but also in the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The path behind Vlatko's house and in front of the warehouse, there was a machine gun there, because when they were retreating, of course, they moved toward Upper Ahmici. So that the sounds of gunfire simply rang out, and we heard gunfire in that part as well.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry, the microphone is not on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you see the Muslim villagers leaving?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we could see some Muslims who lived in Zume were leaving, and Enver Sehic told me that he was going to Zenica, that he was going to his native village. I noticed that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: When did the gunfire stop on that first day? You said that you heard it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it stopped at about 16.00 hours, sometime after 4 p.m., and towards the end of the gunfire, we could see Mehmed Ahmic's house, also known as Sudjuka, burning. His house burnt down and several farm buildings. The cowshed or stable belonging to Miro Josipovic, and Mehmed Ahmic, Sudjuka's uncle's stable also burnt down. I was told about the stables later, but we could see the house burning.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Do you know who took part in the conflict? Did the Croats from the village or from any part of the village take part in that first clash?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Croats from that part of the village certainly did not participate in that clash, because they had no idea what it was all about. We learned on that day, while the conflict was still going on, that a checkpoint had been set up by the Muslims below our cemetery, that they had even dug a trench in the cemetery itself, and that they had cut off the communication. People were going from Busovaca to the war theatre in Jajce at that time, and allegedly they stopped a military police vehicle and confiscated their vehicle as well as four automatic rifles, at least that's what people said afterwards. So that that unit probably responded to all this, and there was a clash between the forces of that unit and the Muslim army which had set up the roadblock.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Do you know, after this conflict, what was done to pacify the situation in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that several meetings were organised. I did not attend these meetings, because I continued my usual everyday tasks since I have my own business. But there was one meeting which was held in front of my house. I was in Vitez, in my restaurant which I own, and my aunt let me know that some people had arrived from Ahmici and Vitez and that I should come home. So I got into my car and went home. On the terrace of my house, I found Fuad and Junuz Berbic, Kalco Sulejman, who was the representative of the Muslim people from the town of Vitez, municipality of Vitez, and Sukrija Ahmic. And from our side I found Nenad Santic there, Zoran Kupreskic, who was very good friends with Fuad and Junuz. And Fuad, knowing what Zoran was like, that he was highly respected, tried to establish contact and simply to prevent an escalation of this event, because this had been done by two armies which were not local; they were not local people. The representative of the Croatian people from Vitez was Pero Skopljak, who was also at that meeting. There were talks about restoring confidence. They said that it was not they who had done this, as our neighbours, and at least these representatives told us that they knew that no neighbours, no Croatian neighbours were involved in this clash. We didn't talk long. We drank a bottle of liquor on that terrace and we parted. We were all satisfied. It was agreed that we should start joint guards, joint village guards again after this.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You say that they told you that the Muslims from the village had not taken part in that clash?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you say that you had seen armed men in front of your house that morning whom you recognised?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I did. I said that. But we didn't want to rock the boat at that meeting. We simply wanted to restore confidence in the village, and we wanted to continue living normally.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: During the time the Muslims were not in the village, did you look after their houses? Did you try to protect their property in any way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We organised ourselves so that until their return to the village, we patrolled the village. We were helped by the people from Zume, from Pudzine Kuce, so that -- one patrol, in Atif or Latif Ahmic's house, I can't remember exactly, the son of Hazim Hadzija, who had the mosques, we caught a thief who had come to loot their property, and we reported him duly, and this is all documented at the Vitez police. He was actually a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So you reported this event to the police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't in the patrol at that time; it was another patrol. They were patrolling in that part of the village where our cemetery was, and this was actually Donji or Lower Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: At the entrance to Ahmici, was there some kind of joint guard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, a joint guard was agreed on at the meeting. And since I had attended that meeting, I volunteered, because I wanted matters to improve in the village, so I volunteered to go with the Muslims first and to go to the guard. It wasn't actually a checkpoint; it was simply a guard.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did this guard function well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not for long. Only for a few days. Only a few days. And then everything was interrupted.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: While it was functioning, how many Croats and how many Muslims were guarding that point together?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Two Croats and two Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You say that you were a participant.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was the first participant. It wasn't a roadblock. It was simply a guard.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: After that conflict, you say that the Muslims returned and that the joint guards were set up again for a certain amount of time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What happened next? How did relations develop in the village from that point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we went on working in the warehouse belonging to Vlatko Kupreskic, and Vlatko worked in my firm at the time, as did Mirjan Kupreskic. He was the head of Veleprodaja in the warehouse in Ahmici at the time. Many Muslims would say hello to us when passing by, but some didn't because, already at that time, some people thought that we were responsible for that, that we had done that. They didn't know the real truth about the matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: When you say "we," you mean the Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I mean the Croat neighbours. But as we were not responsible for the conflict, it occurred because of the barricade at the cemetery, it is obvious that individual Muslims thought that perhaps it might have been some of the neighbours that did this, but that was not the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You said that some people would turn their heads away from you. What about the Muslims that you were friends with? Did you remain on good terms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we remained on very good terms with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did anything change in the village between the two conflicts? Was there trench digging on one or the other side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, one week, we noticed trench digging below the forest belonging to Franjo Sakic and above Redzib Ahmic's house. We got ready, that is to say, I myself, Mirko Vidovic, Zoran Kupreskic, I think that Ivica Covic was there, and we went along the road from the old house of Franjo Sakic. Through the forest on the upper side of the trench that was being dug, we met Suad Ahmic, who was tending to his sheep and making the move from Franjo Sakic's forest. When we left Franjo Sakic's forest, when we emerged from the forest on the upper side, we saw that the trench was being dug by Suad Ahmic's brother, Omer, and Kermo, but I really don't know his surname. Both of them were underage at the time. They were 16 or 17. They were minors. They had an automatic rifle by their side, and when we approached the trench, Kermo took up this automatic rifle and drew it closer towards him. We asked them what they were digging, and they answered that they were digging a sort of shelter. However, we moved on towards Ahmici, towards the section where the upper mosque is located, and we saw that on the high ground there, which exists above the upper mosque and a basin, a water basin which supplies water for Muslim and Croatian houses, that there was another trench which had been dug and had an entrance from the top towards the front and that it had a very good view towards the school building and the mosque and Vlatko Kupreskic's warehouse, whereas the first trench had a very good view of the Kupreskic houses, all of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What time was this when you noticed that the trenches were being dug? When was this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was Sunday, perhaps somewhere in December. There wasn't any snow yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you consider that the trenches should be filled in? Did you react?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes, there was reaction, and a meeting was called in the school of Ahmici. I did not attend the meeting, but I do know that Redzib Ahmic took it upon himself to go and fill in the trench.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Were the trenches filled in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, the one that we reached, the trench we reached which was being dug, that it was filled in by Redzib Ahmic. As to the second trench above the mosque, that was not filled in.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did anything else happen in that period between the two conflicts, in the interim?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I was working quite normally for my firm, and Vlatko and Mirjan Kupreskic worked there too. We were the best suppliers of pickled goods for the Vitez municipality, and then we distributed these goods after the meeting, that is to say, at the beginning of November, which means that this food for winter was handed out to all the municipalities. All these preserved goods went round to the municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What was your company, your firm, called?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I established it in 1991, I think that it was January 1991, it was called Stefani-Bosna because I worked with a Stefani firm from Ljubljana and another Stefani company in Athens. In 1992, between the two conflicts, I changed the name, and it became known as the Sutra Company.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: How was this firm registered, for what kind of business?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was registered for the catering industry, for tourism, and for trading.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Where was Mirjan Kupreskic employed between the two conflicts, in what part of your company?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mirjan Kupreskic, at that time, worked in the wholesale department, Veleprodaja in Ahmici, in Vlatko Kupreskic's warehouse, up until my return from Germany.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So he worked on the selling of these goods wholesale, the goods that you had acquired?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They were wholesale sales.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Where did you stock the goods that were intended for sale in this manner?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, most of the goods were stored in Vlatko Kupreskic's warehouse, and everything that was not able to go there, I stored in my own home because I have a sort of business area in my own house for storage.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: When you say you had a business area in your house, was that a storage space as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was storage space, and I had a small shop there at one time, but I closed that because there was a shop down below. So we used it as a storage space, as a sort of small warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: The selling of these winter preserves that you were engaged in, which began after the conflict in November 1992 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: -- was this permitted by the HVO and the municipal organs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The HVO and the municipality asked all the companies to make bids and say which kind of goods and winter preserves they had, under which terms. They were sort of tenders. We were selected as being the best offer available. We started purchasing the goods straightaway, and we would send the goods on to our main buyers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: The goods were sold to the Muslims as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, to the Muslims as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And the Muslims bought your goods?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they did buy them. It was because of them that we would get vegetable fat, which was packed in packages of 12 kilogrammes, and as --

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kupreskic. I think we can take a break at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. We will take a break.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. Kupreskic, I am going to hand to you some documents which are excerpts from some bills from your books.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Would the usher please hand this to the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D100/2.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Kupreskic, are these notes taken from this notebook of yours where you recorded your notes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they have been taken from my notebook.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: From this, we can see that you began on the 2nd of November, 1992 with the sales?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: The names that are stated here, Hamzo Kavazovic from Vrhovine?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Then we have Dzemal Viteskic from Bukve, Mustafa Varupa?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Petar Mecava, Senad Livnjak, Safet Melkic, Muharem Sivro, Zijad Tarahija?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Avdo Burak, Nasid Salkic, Melkic, I think it's Safet. Are they Croats or Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They are all Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Therefore, these sales were that the preserves were insured at a lower price for both Muslims --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: -- and for Croats alike?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These were the first people, that is to say, each village had its own man. He was in charge, and he would collect quantities necessary for the village. They already had the prices that were offered. We would prepare the goods, and we would send them the goods on time. This can be seen from the payments that were made afterwards for the goods taken over. We were to have distributed these goods a little earlier, but we were slowed down somewhat by the first conflict, the first case that occurred in Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Here we have your own payments, but I don't think we need all these papers and documents at this point. The people from Ahmici, did they buy goods at your place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they did, but a smaller portion at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Tell us, when these goods were distributed, you said that Mirjan Kupreskic took part in distribution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Mirjan Kupreskic did take part in the distribution because all the goods that came to the warehouse, he would record the goods that came in and would plan the distribution, and myself and Vlatko Kupreskic would help him out. But there were a number of poorer families, and so if necessary, the vegetable fat that was packed in packages of 12.5 kilogrammes, if they had to be broken up into smaller packages for payment, then Mirjan Kupreskic would break up the larger packages into the smaller packages, so that people who didn't have as much money could purchase the vegetable fat nonetheless.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Were people able to pay for goods later on or did they have to pay immediately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The prices were very low, and you had to pay for the goods immediately when you took them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Kupreskic, we now come to March, that is to say, April 1993. Where was your family in March and April 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My family, in March 1993, was in Germany, in the town of Essen. They were registered there as refugees and had a refugee card because all those people who stayed on a little longer in Germany were treated that way. They were treated as refugees and had their refugee status. My brother gave them his apartment to live in.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Very well. Did you decide to bring your family back to Bosnia and why?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, my youngest son, who was eight years old at the time, phoned me from Germany and told me at one point that he was homesick and that unless I came to fetch him, he would jump off the third floor of the building. I said to him immediately, "Don't worry, son. Your daddy is coming to get you." So on the 13th of March, 1993, I bought a plane ticket in Split. I got on the plane of Croatian Airlines and flew to Dusseldorf. I thought I'd stay there for a little while and perhaps take my children because I didn't want them to miss a school year. They were enrolled in a German school, but I was told that they would have to spend at least two months in the school in Vitez for that scholastic year to be recognised. On the 13th of March, 1993, I flew out there. I talked to my wife. I stayed a little under a month. As my wife's "duldung" visa expired on the 13th of April, 1993, it was necessary to prolong it for a further six months which meant up to the 14th of October, 1993, so that if there were any problems of any kind up there, she could return quite normally and not have to ask for refugee status to be accorded her once again. We decided that I was to go on the journey with my children and to take the car that I had left up there on the 9th of April, 1993 and that my wife should remain and extend her "duldung" visa from the 14th and to use my return ticket issued by Croatia Airlines and come to Split. So I came home with my children. I made use of the next day, the following day, to enrol them in school so that they could start going to school regularly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What date did you return to Pirici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I returned to Pirici on the 10th.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: The 10th of April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the 10th of April.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You enrolled your children in the school, and they started going to school regularly until the beginning of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they went to school until the beginning of the conflict, and they did so on the 15th of April. My son, who was the youngest, went quite normally, and as it was a school with only three forms in Ahmici, he was enrolled in the first form.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: When did you go to fetch your wife?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My wife contacted me on the 13th in the evening, saying that she was to go to have her "duldung" visa extended on the 14th, and that same afternoon, she would have a flight via Zagreb to Split. I said I would meet her in Split. We checked the flight, the time the flight was to arrive, and it was to arrive at 21.20.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Who did you go to Split with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I invited my relative, Vlatko Kupreskic. I said to him, "We have business to do in Split, so let's combine business and pleasure and do what we have to do and then fetch my wife and bring her home."

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What vehicle did you use?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 14th, in the morning, we set off with a Yugo 45. It was my Yugo 45. This vehicle was registered in my wife's name. We passed along the stretch of road leading toward Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What colour was your Yugo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Yugo was light blue, pale blue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Which vehicle did you use to come back from Germany?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I returned in a Mercedes 240 which was dark green.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Why did you take the Yugo, which is a small car?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I used it for the simple reason that I didn't want to use the Mercedes on such bad roads, because we had to pass along 26 kilometres of macadam road near Gornji Vakuf or Uskoplje, and the macadam which was -- there was another stretch with the mountain of Vrana, some 50 kilometres long, which was macadam, and that's why I used the vehicle I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Which road did you take?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We took the Vitez-Novi Travnik road. We came across the first HVO checkpoint, which was set up at the crossroads, one road leading to Bugojno and the other in the direction of Gornji Vakuf. They suggested, the people manning the checkpoint suggested that unless we had some kind of commitment, it might be better for us to return home. However, since my wife was to arrive on that day, we decided to continue. Some four or five kilometres down the road from the roadblock, we were stopped by a soldier belonging to the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. He had a green fez on his head; it's a kind of cap Muslims wear. So I give him a lift. I asked him, simply to make conversation, to have a chat with him, and he said he was from Gornji Rovna and that he had been manning the army of B and H roadblock at Opara, above Novi Travnik, on the road leading to Gornji Vakuf. I told him that they had warned us at the last checkpoint that we might have some problems, so I asked him, if there were any problems, to help us. He said that everything would be all right. That's how it was. When I arrived at the checkpoint, there were perhaps some 12 to 15 vehicles there; most of them were cargo vehicles rather than small vehicles. There was a ramp across the road. There was a school on the right-hand side. There were a lot of soldiers at the roadblock, soldiers of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I passed this column, the queue, and arrived at the ramp. We stopped, and the young man got out. This car had only two doors, and he was sitting in the back, so when he managed to get out of the car they saw that he was a colleague of theirs, so they didn't ask us any questions. They simply lifted the ramp, and we continued. We drove through a wood, arrived at the village of Sebesic, where there was another HVO checkpoint. There I noticed that there were up to 30 vehicles queuing, and I noticed that most of these belonged to the Kalen company. They were all tank trucks. They stopped us again, and they told us we should not continue. However, I asked this man and said, "Well, now that I've come this far, why shouldn't I go on?" So he let me through, but at my own responsibility. I drove to Gornji Vakuf and then to Makljen. There was yet another HVO checkpoint there, and they told us that we had to take the macadam road to the mountain of Vran if we had to go in the direction of Split. Since this road was very bad indeed, I suggested to Vlatko that we should try to take the road to Jablanica instead, the proper road. So we arrived at another HVO checkpoint at Rumboci. They stopped us and asked us where we were going. We said we were going to Split. We asked them if there was any traffic. They said the vehicles were very few and far between, and they had no reports of any problems on that road. So we continued. We arrived at an elevation maybe three kilometres further on from that checkpoint, and there was a checkpoint there which had been set up by the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina with a big green flag and a black flag on which there was a skull. We were stopped by the army manning that checkpoint, but then I was recognised by the man whom two days before that I had given a lift to up to that checkpoint, so that they didn't even ask to see our documents. The young man let us continue on our way. We arrived to a point below Jablanica where there was another checkpoint manned by the army of B and H near a bridge that had been destroyed and they didn't stop us. They let us pass through. In Dreznica, another seven or eight kilometres further on, there was yet another B and H army checkpoint where they stopped us, checked our documents, and let us pass through without any problems. We continued on our way in the direction of Metkovic. We arrived at Pocitelj and decided to have a drink there to refresh ourselves. There we met a friend of ours, a Muslim, Fadil Sipcic, who was driving a freight vehicle, a truck, transporting some goods, and he was going to Vitez. Since we were old friends and he would often come to my restaurant, we had a chat, we joked a little, he asked us how the road was, we had a drink, and then we continued each on our way. We went on in the direction of Metkovic. We arrived in Metkovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We are wondering if it would be more appropriate to speed up the proceedings by doing without all these details.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. However, this is a very important part of the defence of Vlatko Kupreskic and of our defence as well because we saw the last time, when Mrs. Ankica Kupreskic was testifying, that the Prosecutor tried to challenge many details in her statement so that this statement by Ivica Kupreskic is simply complementing that witness, and we shall see how the Prosecutor will respond, since this is the road which one day before the conflict and the return of the family one day before the conflict broke out. Besides, this part of the testimony is significant because we wish to show that in that part of Bosnia and Herzegovina the situation was already very tense, that there were a lot of soldiers around, that checkpoints had been set up every few kilometres, so that the situation was certainly not normal, and it shows the presence of large numbers of soldiers and increased control of the entry into the Lasva River Valley.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mrs. Glumac, it can be done much more quickly. The witness has been giving evidence for nine minutes about this journey, and it could be summarised. You could summarise the fact that there were roadblocks, but the fact that he met a friend and had a drink really isn't going to take us very much further.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we wish to show that Vlatko Kupreskic, when they met this person, Fadil Sipcic, that he's going to call this man as his witness, and that's why he was mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Perhaps we can proceed more quickly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will try to speed up.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Very well. So you passed along this path, did you finally arrive in Split?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we arrived in Split. We bought some goods at the market, at the Split market. We put the goods -- and these were jeans, actually -- we put them in the boot of our car, and then we went to the airport in the evening. My wife had arrived by that plane, which landed at about half past 9.00 in the evening. We left Split and went to Baska Voda, to Mr. Radoslav Simovic and his wife Marica. He lives in Baska Voda; he has a house there. We spent that night in his house, and the following morning at about 6.00 a.m. We continued on our way via Vrgorac to Ljubuski and Capljina. We arrived in Capljina. In Capljina we had breakfast, and we tried to make a telephone call to contact our families; however, all the lines were down in the direction of Central Bosnia. We went on in the direction of Mostar, but in the village of Zitomislici, there was an HVO checkpoint where they would not let us go on in the direction of Mostar but told us to go to Citluk, Siroki Brijeg, Posusje, Tomislavgrad, and over Mt. Vran. There were checkpoints there again. We went back to Prozor, Makljen, Gornji Vakuf. In Gornji Vakuf there was already a queue of vehicles which had been stopped, and people suggested that we should not continue along that way because they were stopping vehicles in the woods further up that road. However, since my children had been left at home alone, we decided to go on nonetheless. We arrived at another checkpoint in Sebesic, and there was already a long queue of vehicles. The queue was about two and a half kilometres long. Sebesic is in a wood. So I drove by this queue and arrived at the head of the queue. The person who stopped me was very angry --

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Whose was the checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was an HVO checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: How far is Sebesic from Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sebesic is perhaps some 35 kilometres away from Vitez. And we were stopped there, our documents were checked, and he told us we could not go on because there were some problems down below through the Muslim territory, and there had been murders in that part of the wood before. I told him that my children were at home alone, and that we would try to go on, and that we would take responsibility for this. So I managed with great difficulty to persuade him to let us pass, but he told me, "At least let me take your names down, because you will probably be killed on this road."

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you get any information regarding the situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that's the information he gave us. He said that the Totic case had happened that morning. We hadn't heard about it before, since we were away. I think that the tensions had increased precisely because of that case, as he told me, the thing that took place at the checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: In one section, you passed by the same road -- let me just ask you something, please. Was the situation at the checkpoints -- had it changed since the day before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it had changed. There were far more soldiers than had been present the day before, which means that the situation was more tense. It was in the afternoon hours of the 15th.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So you passed the roadblock and went on towards Vitez. What happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To Vitez, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You say you passed the checkpoint and the Muslim part?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I passed the Muslim part at Opara, where I had left the young man up at the checkpoint. There were no vehicles there any more. The ramp had been lifted. There was just one policeman standing on the left-hand side with a vehicle, and he stopped us. He was a young man. He asked me where I was coming from and whether the road had been opened. I had to do the best I could at that point, because I was afraid, too, and I said that I knew nothing about the road, but that they had let me pass because I had had some problems.
