I said that my wife's mother had died and that I was going from Germany to attend the funeral. He didn't open any of my documents, my papers, and he said, "Well, I don't want to keep you any longer, you may pass through." I gave him some chocolates, I believe, and we continued on our route. We came home. It was about 6.30 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And where did you go then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I say, I went home. My father came out, my aunt came out to say hello to my wife. My wife just left the small bag she was carrying with her, and she wanted to go and see her own family as soon as possible. She had a lot of family. She wanted to see them all because they hadn't seen each other for one year and 17 days. And we went to Krcevine, which is her village. She saw everybody there except her brother, and her brother was killed on the fourth day in the conflict. We didn't stay up there long. We went back home. It was about 8.00 in the evening when we returned, and my relatives and friends came to visit. They wanted to say hello to my wife first. We chatted, we had a few jokes, and we talked about the journey we had had both ways.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: How long did your journey last, in fact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From 6.00 in the morning to 6.30 in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And how far is it from Vitez to Split?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From Vitez to Split, going by the road we took, if you mean the road we took, it is almost 400 kilometres by that road. But there were a lot of checkpoints, a lot of barricades.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And what about the road by Kupres?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The road across Kupres is 220 kilometres long -- to Split, that is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Why couldn't you go that way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we couldn't take that road for the simple reason that Kupres, at that time, was held by the Serbian forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Very well, then. So in the evening you said your friends and relations came by to see you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Do you remember who these people were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I know that Mirjan and Zoran came. We left Vlatko at his own house, but his wife came and so did his mother. Zoran and Mirjan with their wives came. Gordana Vidovic came to see us, and the other refugees who were put up in my brothers's houses, Josip and Branko, Manda and Marica and her mother-in-law. Mirko Sakic came by. Miro Vidovic came, Franjo's son. Miroslav Pudza also came by. They liked to joke with me because I had got married again, for the second time, so they made jokes about that. So there was a lot of coming and going. Zoran didn't stay too long because he had guests at his own house.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Do you remember, you said that you discussed the journey up from Split and that you talked about Germany and so on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Were there any discussions about any information on the situation in Vitez, for example?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not about information on the situation in Vitez, but we did mention the Totic case, because I myself was surprised when I heard what had happened, so I asked whether anybody could enlighten me as to the details, just to give me some more information about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: When did the people leave your house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, everybody left a little before 12.00. About 12.00, we were alone.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did anything happen during the night, or did you go to bed as you usually do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My wife and I and children went to sleep in the normal way. The children had gone to bed earlier. The next morning, a little after 4.00 a.m., I remember very well Dragan Vidovic came, and Stipan's -- there is another Dragan, of course -- and he woke me up, and he told us that there was the possibility of an attack by the Muslim side and that we should urgently take our families to a shelter.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: I apologise, but could you tell us again who came?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dragan Vidovic, Stipan's son Dragan.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Therefore, that is one particular individual?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, one person.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Very well; thank you. You may continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I asked him where I should take them, because they had not been there before and there were alerts before that. And he said that that best thing would be for them to go to the shelter by Jozo Vrebac's place, the Trajanovski shelter. I woke my wife up. I told her that she should get up quickly and get the children ready and go to the shelter there. She told me that she had still not had enough sleep. I said, "Well, there are probably some problems, and you should get up and go." I said, "This isn't Germany, you know." So she got up, she got the children ready, she collected a few things together, and a little before 5.00 we started out towards the shelter belonging to Jozo Vrebac. I took them through the depression by Pudzine Kuce up to Zume, up to about Ivica Vidovic's, Jevco's house. I told her that she should continue on with the children alone and go up to Jozo Vrebac's house because she knew where the house was situated. I said to her that I was to go back and warn the refugees once again -- that is to say, the refugees which had been put up in my brothers's houses, Branko's and Josip's house. I woke them up at the same time and told them that they had to go. They told me that they weren't interested in any of that, and that they had experienced many false alarms before that, and that they had already had to leave their own houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What were the names of these refugees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The refugees's name was the (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted), who was put up in my brother Josip's house.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Were there any children with them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were. Both families had children.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Where were their husbands?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Their husbands were up at the front line facing the Serbs near their own village, the Didaci, near Turbe.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Very well; thank you. Please continue and tell us what happened next.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I left my wife at Ivica Vidovic's house, and they went on towards the shelter, whereas I returned back to my own house quickly. Some 50 to 100 metres away from them, as I left them, I met my aunt and uncle first. I met Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic's parents and after them, some 200 metres later, by Pudzine Kuce, I met Zoran and Mirjan with their own families, and Mirjan, who was taking his mother-in-law in a wheelbarrow. She was being taken in a wheelbarrow. I continued, and I was close to Niko Sakic's house at this point, and by Niko Sakic's house I met some soldiers, a group of soldiers, in fact, who were going in the direction of Vlatko Kupreskic's warehouse. And as this was the point where I was to turn off towards the left and take the path across the depression to my own house, they went forward. I arrived in front of my brother Branko's house, and (redacted) and her mother-in-law and children were already ready. I told them to leave immediately, that something was happening, and that I had already seen some armed soldiers. After that, I went to my brother Josip's house, Manda was also ready, and I told them that they had to go too. My aunt, she is now an old woman of 75, she didn't want to leave in the first conflict and said she wasn't going to leave now either, and she said, "If necessary, let them kill me." I nonetheless tried to convince her to leave as well; however, she was joined by the mother-in-law of these two (redacted) women, Luca was her name, and, quite simply, the two of them said that they weren't budging, that they weren't going to leave my house. I then called Vlatko Kupreskic because I thought that somebody had warned him already, and I told him that the situation was tense and that he should leave too. He told me that he had already had a phone call to that effect. So I went out in front of Josip Kupreskic's house -- no, I beg your pardon, first of all, on my own terrace, and I could see it very well, that is to say, I could see the road from my terrace, the road passing beside my own house and Zoran's house. I saw from that vantage point the deployment of some soldiers. I could hear footsteps, the rattling of weapons. I went towards the (redacted) once again, and once again, I saw a group of some four soldiers going behind my own house from the direction of the depression, that is to say, it was a wood or forest. They called me and said, "Hey, you. Come here." I said, "Let me just accompany this family and my own children, take them away." They passed by me, went towards the house belonging to Mirjan's father, Ante, whereas I went into the boiler room of my brother Josip's house, and it was dug deep into the ground from all sides, except one side, of course, and there was no door at all. As it was dark, it was dusk, I sat down on a log, put my hands on my head and said, "God, what's all this going on? Is it possible that I could have brought my family back to a situation of this kind?" Shortly after that, perhaps some five minutes went by, there was loud shooting going on from all sides. We could hear things burning. There was smoke. There were flames. Everything was on fire; that's the impression I got, that everything had been set on fire. I was completely breathless and was deep in that shelter, sitting deep in the shelter. At one particular moment --

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. Kupreskic, may I interrupt you at this point and ask you to show us on the map where the depression is located, which road you took towards your own house, where you saw the army, and which way the soldiers went in the direction of your house, which route they took?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it's like this. This is my house (indicating). I had taken my family from our house, this way, along this road past this wood, and that is where the depression is. That's the depression here (indicating). This is Niko Sakic's house (indicating). Then I continued with them along this road and went to this place here (indicating). That's where I left my family because that is Ivica Vidovic's house, nickname Jevco. They continued on their own to the shelter, which is located here (indicating), whereas I returned back along this route. Somewhere along that route, I met Zoran and Mirjan's parents, and Zoran and Mirjan themselves, I met somewhere here, in this region (indicating). I had caught up with the soldiers here who were moving towards the direction of the warehouse, this direction (indicating), whereas I took a left turn towards the house. This is my brother Branko's house (indicating). I first went to his house to warn (redacted) and then continued on up to Josip's house and warned Manda. Then I went down towards my own house and the bottom of it, because the entrance, the front door, is below, and from the main terrace, that's where I went. I wanted to convince my aunt to go to the shelter as well, but she really didn't want to. I hid here (indicating) and met the soldiers, the group of soldiers, here who were moving towards Mirjan's father's house. They called out to me. They continued along this path, and I went into the garage here.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you see the direction from which the soldiers were coming?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw that from the terrace, while I was still on the terrace trying to convince my aunt to leave. They had probably been deployed here and were coming from this direction (indicating), between our houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: The four soldiers who you said called out to you, can you tell us from which direction they came?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they might have come through this part or across this meadow or they might simply have come this way (indicating). They might have even used this path (indicating). I really don't know which path they used.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Could you please mark some spots on this aerial photograph that you talked about?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked D101/2.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You may sit down. Please, could you show the place at which you saw the soldiers and the direction in which they left, as far as you were able to see? So just an arrow pointing in the direction they went.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw the soldiers here (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Could you show this on the overhead projector so that we could see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is it (marks). They were moving in this direction toward the warehouse (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What direction did you move in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This direction (marks), through the depression.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: The soldiers you saw from the terrace --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: -- from what direction did they come?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They came from this direction (marks).

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And the four soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They arrived from behind my back, so this direction here, from this direction (marks).

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Could you please put a circle around Josip Kupreskic's house in whose shelter or boiler room you hid?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here, this is it (marks).

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Please, could you show the direction or could you put a number 1 next to the direction the soldiers were moving in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Marks)

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: The direction from which you saw the soldiers coming towards your houses, could you mark it number 2?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Marks)

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: The third direction, the direction in which the four soldiers were moving?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Marks)

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: I would now like to show a very short video, only a few minutes, to see where the garage is between the Kupreskic houses and its position. I would like the video to be shown.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. Kupreskic, there is no text, so just tell us what house is shown, where the room is, and what can be seen from the garage in relation to the surrounding houses. (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the garage. This was really planned as a boiler room. It's in my brother's house. None of this stuff was inside then. Since they were in Germany at that time, it was empty.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So the window we saw on the right-hand side, the little window, where does it face?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It looks into my brother's bathroom because the house is on the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Are there any other windows inside?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No, it's all underground. This is the view from the entrance. This is the old house.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Whose house was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's my father's house, Ivo. This is the garage in which Mirjan Santic was brought later, straight ahead. Then the next house is my house; right in front, my house. This is Zoran's house, you can see there, the house of Zoran Kupreskic. Here you can see the house of Sukrija Ahmic which was burnt down, and Sakib Ahmic's house was in front of it. The house on the left-hand side is the house of Zoran's father, Ante Kupreskic. Mirjan lived upstairs on the upper floor of that house.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Who lived in the lower floor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My aunt and uncle.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: The road, the lane, is the main road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's the main road leading to our houses. It goes between my house and Zoran's house from the -- this is where the soldiers came, from the direction of the warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And this area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was my garage.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: But I mean this house, what is this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is used for curing meat. This is the old house.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: The road leading to the depression would be beside this old house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Kupreskic, from the place where you were --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: -- you were able to see the surrounding houses and part of the area in the direction of Sakib Ahmic's house and the house of his son Sukrija --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: -- and some of the area around Vlatko Kupreskic's warehouse?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Not just the warehouse but the surrounding area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, my house is in the way, blocking off a view of the warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Where is Branko Kupreskic's house in relation to the houses we saw on the video? Where is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Branko Kupreskic's house is behind the boiler room and more to the right, looking in the direction of my house. So it's more to the right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What then happened? You said you heard gunfire. You were in the boiler room. What did you see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in the boiler room, and some ten minutes later, after the gunfire started, I tried to peer out to see, if possible, at least something because I was, of course, afraid of being hit by a bullet. The first thing I saw was that Sakib Ahmic's house was on fire. Right after that, the house of his son, Sukrija Ahmic, burst into flames. I saw this, and I saw flames and smoke. I heard gunfire. I heard the crackle of the fires, and, of course, I went back. For reasons of safety, I didn't stick my head out for long. Then I wondered what to do, and I was desperate because I had brought my family back to this.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Where was the gunfire coming from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was coming from all directions. Since I was inside, I was really unable to gather from which direction it was coming. It was coming from all sides, and I had the feeling that everything was on fire, that there was shooting everywhere. I could understand nothing. I was terrified.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What happened half an hour later?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After half an hour, two soldiers ran into the same boiler room. One was wearing a black uniform and the other was wearing a camouflage uniform. They had automatic rifles with them, and they had rounds of ammunition and several hand grenades. They had black bands over their foreheads, and they had paint on their faces. One of them had an M-48 rifle slung over his shoulder; there was a belt over his shoulder. They hadn't noticed me yet because I was hiding in the corner and it was quite dark. So when they ran in, they probably weren't paying attention to that corner. One of them, the one who was in the black uniform, put his gun away and started taking off the M-48. He told his colleague, "I have just confiscated this gun." Then he noticed me, and he pointed the gun at me and he asked me, "What's your name?" I was terrified. I was out of my wits. He said, "Who do you belong to?" I said, "I belong to you." I didn't know who they were. I said, "I belong to you." He said, "What's your name," and I said, "My name is Ivica." He said, "Where is your house," and I said, "Over there, some 50 metres away." He said, "Do you have anything to drink in your house," and I said, "Yes, I do." So he said, "Go and fetch the drinks." I said, "I don't dare. I have to run some 50 metres." He said, "You're afraid of running cross 50 metres, and we are at the front line." So they simply chased me. They made me go to my house. I knocked on my aunt's window, on the right-hand side of the house, and she handed me a bottle of brandy. I ran back and I gave it to them. They had two or three drinks, they stayed for about ten minutes, and then I asked them who they were. They said, "You don't know who we are?" I said, "No, I don't know. Who are you?" They said they were Jokers. They said, "Don't you know who the Jokers are? They are a special unit of the military police." They didn't stay there long. They left again, and I stayed there. The gunfire went on. It was very intense. In the meantime, when they arrived, they said that Mirjan Santic had been killed. So I asked, "Which Mirjan Santic," and they said, "Mirjan Santic from Santici." I said, "Is it possible that he has been killed?" They said, "Yes," not far from our houses. Then they left again. They went outside. I stayed inside. I didn't dare go out. From time to time, I stuck my head out to see what was burning. That's all. I watched to see whether my house was on fire because I could see it. It was right across the way. At about 10.00 in the morning or it may have been a little later than 10.00, those two soldiers and a third one carried Mirjan Santic. He had been a heavy-built man, about 110 kilogrammes in weight. When I saw him, I really couldn't believe it. They brought him to my garage, which I pointed out to you. They called to me, and I ran out to help them. We put him on a ladder, on a ladder, and we laid his hands across his chest. They said to me that I had to find someone urgently to transport the corpse in the direction of Pudzine Kuce. I went back to the boiler room, I stayed there for some 15 minutes, and when there was a lull in the gunfire -- it didn't stop completely but it became more quiet because sometimes it was more intense and sometimes it was less intense and then it would become more intense again -- so I ran out and set off in the direction of the depression to find someone to help me because I was frightened. I thought they might do something to me if we didn't move Mirjan's body to where they said. I came to the edge of the depression, and I met Nikola Omazic, who was a little tipsy at that moment, and it was quite noticeable because he was staggering. I said that Mirjan Santic had been killed and that he had been brought to my garage, and I told him to look for someone to help us carry him at least to the depression. He said, "Let's go, the two of us." I said, "How can the two of us do it on our own? He is very heavy." So he followed me. We came to the garage. We took hold of the ladder, one on each side, and very quickly, we passed behind my father's old house in the direction of the depression. From the depression, Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic came out and Dragan Vidovic, and they took over the corpse, together with Nikola Omazic, and took him to Niko Sakic's house. I returned once again to the same boiler room because I thought I would be safest there, safer than anywhere else, and I stayed there until about 1.00. My aunt had already opened the window, and she told me that she would prepare some food for the children and for family and that I should take it to them. Somewhere around 1.00, she prepared the meal, and I took the food and went past the depression again, right up to the shelter. When I passed through the depression, passed by the depression, I saw Zoran and Mirjan there again and Mirko Sakic, and there was some other people there as well, but the ones I mentioned were certainly there. I said that I was taking some food for my family, and I went to the shelter. I took the food. My wife came out of the shelter. I gave her everything I had brought with me. The children came out for a little while. We kissed. I said that I was to return home again so that if any of the houses were set alight, I was the only one that could put the fire out, and that my aunt was there as well and that she was an elderly woman, and if anything happened to her, then I could evacuate her as well. The army didn't return to that part, and the shooting went on towards the middle region of Ahmici, so it wasn't as close as it was in the morning. I stayed there. My aunt once again prepared some food for us. At about 6.00 p.m., at about 6.00 in the evening, I took some food again and some clothing that was necessary. I took a few blankets so that the children could use them to cover themselves with during the night and went out towards the shelter again. From the depression, Zoran and Mirjan went with me and Mirko Sakic as well. We went to the shelter together. We saw our families, first of all, my own family and Mirjan's family, who were located in the Trajanovski house, whereas Zoran's family was put up in Milutin Vidovic's house. After that, we went to Milutin Vidovic's house and continued our journey onwards towards the depression. All this lasted for about an hour, perhaps a little longer.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. President, perhaps we could take a break here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We can continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You said that you returned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we returned to the depression that evening, and on that evening I again went to my houses, and I was there until about half past 7.00. The gunfire could be heard constantly, but more in the lower part of Ahmici, where the mosque was. At about half past 7.00 in the evening, a terrible detonation could be heard. After that, there was extremely intense gunfire, and an hour later, since it was dark and we had no idea what was going on, we were told that the minaret of the mosque had crashed and that the mosque had been blown up, actually. At about 9.00 p.m., perhaps a little before that, some soldiers arrived. When we asked them where they had come from, they said they were from Novi Travnik, the Novi Travnik police. They said that they would spend that night there simply because they wanted to go home, there was no shooting that night. There were only some fires still burning.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: When you say "we," who are you referring to? You say "we."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise. I was there on my own. I didn't follow them. They left. I don't know where they went, but I went back to the depression; it was still night. Mirjan and Zoran were still there, Mirko Sakic was there. There where some other people. In the evening we would go to the hayloft, to my father's hayloft together. Some people slept in the hayloft. I went to my father's house and slept for half an hour or so, because this was a terrible misfortune that had taken place nearby.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: When you say the hayloft, what are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I'm referring to my father's cowshed. He had some hay upstairs to feed the cattle and the livestock.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: This cowshed, was it the closest building to the depression?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That was the building closest to the depression and behind the cowshed there is a smaller depression, and then there is this big depression.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You said that some people slept in the hayloft?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Do you remember who was there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, people came and went. No one slept there for long, because who could sleep after everything that had happened that day?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you see Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes, they would come up to the hayloft, and I left them to go into my father's house.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: On the next day, what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the next day, the gunfire started only at about half past 10.00 in the morning. There was intense gunfire again, but it was directed toward Gornji or Upper Ahmici, more toward Upper Ahmici. And we could hear it until the evening, and then it fell silent at about 19.00 hours in the evening, perhaps. But it was almost at the end of Gornji or Upper Ahmici, so that there was less shooting around our houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you see Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic on that day, and where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic again. They had retreated from the hayloft into the depression, and again I took food for the children prepared by my aunt for the family. She had prepared a larger quantity of food so that I could share it with those who didn't have any. So I went to the shelter about three times that day, and in the evening when I had come back to the houses I was told that the Croatian refugees from all the shelters in the area had had to flee in the direction of Donja Rovna, because it was rumoured that the Mujahedin had broken through the front line at Krtina-Mahala.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did your family flee as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, my family fled, together with these people, until the evening, until about 11.00 p.m. I didn't even know -- I was told then that they had all had to leave. I don't remember who it was that told me this because quite a lot of people would come to the hayloft and then go back. It was the people from Pudzine Kuce and Zoran and Mirjan.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Where did you spend the second night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We spent it at the houses again, on the second night, I slept a little in my father's house, some people slept in the hayloft. Zoran and Mirjan were in the hayloft too. The following morning, as soon as dawn broke, at about perhaps 6.00 or half past 6.00, I went toward Jozo Vrebac's shelter and then took the road to Donja Rovna along which my family had fled. I found my family in Pero Santic's house in Donja Rovna, and Mirjan's wife and children too.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So this was Pero Santic's house which is located in Donja Rovna; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the house of Pero Santic, which was situated in Donja Rovna.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: After that, did you stay in Donja Rovna, or did you return to the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I stayed with my family for a certain time, perhaps until 1.00 or half past 1.00, and then I went back home again because they had told us that my aunt was cooking food for us, and there weren't many people there, and they could take care of themselves there. So I just went to fetch some foodstuffs for them to use when preparing their own meals.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: On the third day, was there any gunfire heard in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the third day, there was no gunfire in Ahmici, but we could hear gunfire in Gornja Pirici. So on the third day, gunfire could be heard from Gornja Pirici.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you move away from your house on the third day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we, that is I, didn't go anywhere. I just went to Donja Rovna twice, and I was there again until perhaps 17.00 hours, 17.30. So between 5.00 and 6.00 p.m. some policemen came by, and they had a number of civilians from Vitez with them. They were all wearing civilian uniforms, none of them were wearing any kind of uniforms. They made all of us in the area go to Pirici, to the village. When we arrived in the village, Slavko Papic told us where to dig trenches. He told me to dig a trench. I don't know about the others, but Slavko Papic told me where I had to dig a trench. We were supposed to create a defence line there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Was there any gunfire coming toward the place where you arrived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not then, but there was a shot or two during the night. We spent the whole night there. We dug a little. It was quite cold, quite cold. It even drizzled a little bit that evening.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Who went with you to this defence line? Who was brought there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, all of us who had been there, Mirko Sakic, Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic, Milutin Vidovic, Samija, Dragan Samija. There were quite a few of us. There was quite a large number of us. Anyone they found at the houses, and those whom they didn't find that day, they found the next day. At one moment I asked whether I could go to fetch some warm clothing for the people who had arrived from Vitez not knowing where they were going, but they didn't allow me to go back.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What road did you take to Gornja Pirici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We went over the fields from my house directly toward Gornja Pirici. When we were crossing the fields, then we saw, in front of the house of Enver Sehic, Enver was dead. His son, his child, was dead. Zoran Kupreskic then experienced a terrible shock when he saw the child that had gone to school with his son until the day before.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: How did he react?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had the impression that he had a nervous breakdown. He could not eat anything for 15 days. It was really hard for him, especially since we were very, very good friends with Enver.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: When you went to Gornja Pirici, did you stay there for a prolonged period of time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remained in Pirici for about ten days, and then I received an order to go to Gornji Ahmici, Upper Ahmici, to the line there. Of course I went there, and I spent about two and a half months there, and then I was brought back to Pirici, to Mustafa Strmonja's house, where I stayed until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So you spent the entire war, in fact, in your village, or rather, above your village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, above my village.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Can you say whether you know when you were actually mobilised, when your name was put on the list? Do you remember if the list was drawn up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Believe me, I really don't know whether there was a list or who made it. All I know is that anyone who was a squad leader had to make a list of the men and what trench they were assigned to. Whether there was anyone who made a general list, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And this war was mainly in the trenches, you spent it mainly in the trenches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this part of the line where I was in Pirici, never moved. It was there all the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Can you say when you found out about what had happened in Ahmici and the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Well, when did you find out how many victims there had been, what the extent of the destruction and killing was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I heard about it some ten days later, when the corpses were collected. So I found out only about ten days later that there had been really a lot of victims, not only in the lower part but also in the upper part of Ahmici. But believe me, I still don't know even today exactly how many were killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: The goods in your warehouse, you said it was your company's goods, mainly in Vlatko Kupreskic's warehouse and partly in your house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: How were those goods transported?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was transported in trucks to the warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Tell us, what was the value of the goods on the 15th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, an assessment would be up to 150.000 German marks.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Tell us, did you get any shares because you were a participant of the war in this way, as you have described it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never received any shares.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What about your family?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My wife did, my father did, and my aunt, who is 75 now, got some. But I didn't get any.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Tell us, after the end of the war, did Mirjan Kupreskic continue working at your company?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Mirjan Kupreskic continued working. As soon as the company started working, Mirjan started working straightaway then, and he began working in the warehouse in Vitez. He was the head of Velaprodaja Wholesale. When I returned from Germany he moved from Velaprodaja to Ahmici, to Vitez, and the retail trade there because he had his own -- I had my own shop, and he worked in an office there. He worked for about a week before the actual conflict broke out.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And who took the place of Mirjan Kupreskic in the Velaprodaja feature in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was Vlatko Kupreskic's brother-in-law, Ivica Covic's.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What did you say the man's name was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ivica Covic. He was a native of Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: When did you say that your company began working again? Do you remember the month and the year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was approximately in April 1994. As soon as we obtained our first documents and papers from the HVO that we could leave, then we went to fetch the goods.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: How long did Mirjan work in your company?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mirjan worked in my company until he left for The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: In the meantime, I apologize, did he go abroad with his cultural and arts society?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He went to Austria, to Vienna, and once he went to Switzerland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Do you remember the year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was in 1995. I think it was 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Where do you live now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I now reside in Vitez. In Vitez. It is Petar Svacic Street, without a number, in a new building there where I purchased an apartment about a year and a half ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And where do the families of Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic live?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zoran's family lives one floor above me in a three-room apartment there. We go into the same entrance. Mirjan lives in another section of the apartment building which he, he bought it with a mortgage and has to repay it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Why did you move to Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We went to Vitez for the simple reason that it was fairly difficult to look at the region, and one cannot imagine that there is practically no life there any more. We were all very sorry. We know which of our neighbours had lost their lives. We know which of our own people had lost their lives in that region. Everything had been destroyed, and it was very difficult.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the fact that Mirjan Kupreskic's house, that is to say his father's house, Anto Kupreskic's house, during this conflict, at the beginning of the conflict in 1993, was looted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do know that. I think it was on the third day of the conflict, when Mirjan and Zdravko -- I was in Rovna at the time. Mirjan and Zdravko Vrebac would go to fetch their accordion, because he liked playing the accordion. When he came to his door, it was only his apartment that was looted, because he is on the upper storey of the building. The door had been bashed in, and the cupboard had been broken into, as well as the door to his fridge was off its hinges, and he could just take the door and transport it elsewhere. A leather jacket was taken, some gold jewellery that he had was taken; the essential things of value.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Would you now take a look at a document. And I should like to ask the usher to present the document to the witness. It is 353, Defence Exhibit 353. It is Prosecution Exhibit 353.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. Kupreskic, would you just take a look at the fact under 217. Just one moment, please. It is page 30. Number 217.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Let me ask you, do you know the signature of Mirjan Kupreskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know it very well. He worked with me. He worked in my company, and he would sign all the documents that needed to be signed, so I know his signature well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Would you take a look on the right-hand side, the column where it says "Signature. "

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is not his signature, because he never signed his name in this fashion. Never.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Would you now take a look at what has been recorded in front of that, before that, and that is the time engaged in the unit, that column. It says from the 8th of April, '92, to the 21st of February, '96. Was Mirjan Kupreskic in the HVO during that period of time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Do you know where Zoran worked after the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the war, Zoran worked -- that is to say he continued to be in Vitezit, and it was a company made up of three different departments. There was only one company like Vitezit, but as it was a military factory, many people were sent home to wait for work, and the company was devastated, and as I have three children, I gave him my restaurant, and he was head of the restaurant until the time that he left for The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Who had three children? You had three children, or Zoran?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had three children, but Zoran also had three children, and has three children today.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Tell us, did you work with the Muslims after the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. We started working with the Muslims straightaway after the war because there are good people everywhere, people you can work with. We had a considerable number of friends, and in two -- for a period of two years, I worked with Emir Perenda, and we did some big business together. First of all I imported live sheep from Poland, and there were about 2.300 head of sheep. The next year -- I can check, I can check, but I imported from Australia, sheep from Australia, in 1996 it was -- as I say, I imported a whole shipload, 10.400 head of sheep. They all went for the Reis of the Islamic community for the entire Bosnia-Herzegovina area for their national ceremony and festivity, the Kurban Bajram. So in 1995, this was in 1996.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you give any donations in the form of medicine?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Immediately after the war, I went to Germany, and from Germany I brought medicines back. I brought a kombi van full of medicaments. I had bought this kombi van for myself and loaded it up with medicines, and I transported those medicines to Vitez. Half of this contingent I gave to the health centre in Vitez and the other half I gave to the hospital pharmacy in Travnik, to the Muslims. And this can be seen from the document that I have tendered.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: May I now call upon the usher to present the witness with this document as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Could you tell us whether Mirjan Kupreskic did all this business together with you throughout the entire time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Mirjan Kupreskic worked with me throughout this period.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 102/2, and this document is 103/2.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. Kupreskic, can you confirm that this was issued by the medical centre in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: In gratitude for your donation in medicines?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is the certificate and document that I received from them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: We can't see the stamp clearly here, but on the original document it is more visible, and we can see that it is a stamp of the pharmacy of the medical centre in Travnik; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Kupreskic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: I have no more questions. I should just like to tender Defence Exhibits from number 99/2 to 103/2 be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to point out that we do not have a copy of the videocassette which was shown a little while ago, and we would like to have one. Also, as regards the last document, it has to do with a stamp of the pharmacy or from the hospital, or the pharmacy hospital, but I don't see it. Perhaps we could have a copy of the real original document because it's hard to get an idea when I look at this one.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I can present this document so that it can be seen, and the witness can read the stamp that is the original, but it was not visible on the photocopy, and I have the cassette tape for the Prosecutor here. So perhaps the usher can show the original document, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: No objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: They are admitted in evidence. Counsel Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Mr. President, this witness will be questioned by my colleague, Mr. Par.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Par?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Mr. Kupreskic, I'm going to ask you several questions relating to the accused Vlatko Kupreskic. In your testimony today, you said that, between 1992 and 1993, you were the owner and director of a trading company, which was first called Stefani-Bosna and then changed its name to Sutra. I am now going to give you an order of the Higher Court of Zenica. Would you take a look at page 2 and tell us what the document is about?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked D23/3.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was issued by the Higher Court in Zenica, and it refers to the change in the name of the private trading company for catering and tourism, "Stefani-Bosna, Export/Import Vitez," with full responsibility and headquarters in Vitez. "Petra Mecave" is the street, "bb," and it will function under the new title, the company, a private company for trading, for catering, and tourism, and will be called "Sutra Export/Import of Vitez." On the first side of the decision, we have the signature of the authorised person, Ivica Kupreskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. That is the company that you spoke about and for which Vlatko Kupreskic worked. Will you tell us, between 1992 and 1993, was Vlatko employed in the company the whole time, and what kind of work did he do there? Tell us briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, Vlatko, for the most part, worked -- he is an economist by profession, so he did that type of job. He was my sort of partner and co-owner of the firm at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: In the period between 1992 and 1993, was he employed all the time, and was he perhaps mobilised during that period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In 1992 and 1993, he worked normally. No problems there. At the beginning, that is to say, in the first days after the conflict, he opened a shop of his own in Vitez with his wife. So he sold part of the goods that remained in our warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Was he mobilised in that period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Do you know why he wasn't mobilised?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He wasn't mobilised, first and foremost, because, as a young boy, he had a heart operation. He underwent cardiac surgery. He wasn't even a military-able man in the former Yugoslavia. He didn't do his military service because he was not fit for this health-wise.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Tell us whether Vlatko engaged in any political activities. Was he a member of any political party? Did he have any military authorisations or civilian authorisations or anything of that kind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never noticed anything of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Did you ever see him in a uniform or carrying a gun?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: I would now like to discuss the dates of the 14th and 15th of March when you went to collect your wife who had come back from Germany. You said that you organised the trip as partly a business trip and partly a private trip.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Can you say whether you needed any kind of approval for this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. First of all, we had to have a document from our company stating that we were on a business trip, and then we also had to seek approval from the HVO, that is, from the municipality, to go on a journey.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: I will now show you a document, and I will ask you to comment on it and tell the Court what it refers to.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D24/3.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Can you tell us what this document refers to and why it was necessary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This document is necessary if you are going on a business trip. It is issued by the company, and it says here that "Vlatko Kupreskic and Ivica, as the director and his associate in the firm, are going on a business trip, Vitez --"

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: What's the date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The date is the 13th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Who draws up this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Either I do or Vlatko does, one of us two.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: I would now like to ask you to glance at this second document and to tell us what it refers to.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D25/3.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the document issued by the Croatian Defence Council. This is the document which makes it possible for us to travel as regards the municipality. It is evident here that, on the 13th of April, 1993, Ivica Kupreskic from Vitez, that he has the right to stay away from the 14th to the 24th, and it shows that it's a business trip, Vitez-Split-Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Does this approval bear the stamp of the border crossing and the date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It's the Metkovic border crossing on the 14th of April, 1993. So when leaving Bosnia, this stamp was put on our documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Very well. Did Vlatko have to have the same kind of document if he travelled with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he had to have the same one.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: I will show you another document so that you can tell us whether this is the same kind of document issued for Vlatko.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D26/3.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As you can see, this is also the travel authorisation for the 13th of April, 1993, and it refers to Vlatko Kupreskic from Vitez. The destination is the same. The border crossing is the same, Metkovic, the 14th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Thank you. So you set out on this journey in compliance with this travel authorisation, and you said that you used your Yugo car.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether Vlatko Kupreskic had the same kind of blue Yugo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was the same colour. Everything was the same. It was the same make of car.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Very well. In connection with this journey, you mentioned the route along which you travelled to Split and back. I would now like to ask you to mark the route that you have described for us on this map. Could you please take a felt-tipped pen to mark your route from Vitez to Split and then use another colour to mark your route back. I would like to mention that I have marked Vitez, Pocitelj, Baska Voda, and Split on this map because you mentioned these as reference points.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D27/3.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Marks)

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Very well. If you can use another colour to mark your route back.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Marks)

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. You may sit down. You said that in Pocitelj, you met your friend, Fadil Sipcic, a Muslim, who was returning in the direction of Vitez. Can you tell us what time it was approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It might have been perhaps around half past ten or 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: You also said, in the night from the 14th to the 15th, you stayed at whose house in Baska Voda?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Radoslav Simovic's house and his wife Marica's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Can you tell us who was in the house that night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The three of us: Vlatko, my wife, and I. Then there were Marica and Radoslav and their son. Since it was not in the tourist season, the house is very big and they rent rooms, but they had no guests staying there then.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: You said you arrived in Ahmici at about 18.30 hours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Did you part from Vlatko then? What did you do with the goods in your car?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we arrived in Ahmici at 18.30, we arrived in front of Vlatko's house. We unloaded the jeans that we had brought, and my wife and I went to our house and then to Krcevine.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Can you say what you intended to do with the jeans? Did you have some kind of plan connected with these jeans?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we had done something like this before. Vlatko's sister, Jelina, who lives in Travnik, had a boutique. She had a shop where she sold clothes. Some of these jeans were to be taken to Travnik to her shop in the morning by Vlatko, and we intended to sell the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Can you say who Nevzudin Filipovic is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He is Jelina's husband, Vlatko's sister.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: And she has this boutique?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Did you do business with Nevzudin and Jelina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Now, very briefly, on the 16th of April, when you said that in the morning you telephoned Vlatko telling him to go to the shelter, can you tell us what time it was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was on my return, when I had seen off my wife and children, and I had gone to get the refugees in (redacted). Then I asked my aunt, tried to persuade my aunt to go to the shelter, and then I called Vlatko because I assumed that Dragan Vidovic would wake Vlatko up.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: What time was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps a quarter past five.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Now, another question connected to the cars mentioned here: Please, can you tell us whether, in 1993, you sold a car to Vlatko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I sold him a Mercedes. I think it might have been in June 1993. I know that Vlatko built in a diesel engine in Busovaca at a car mechanic's shop. His name was Sano.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: What colour was the Mercedes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was white.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: He changed the engine. It was an engine using gas, and he changed it into a diesel engine. That was in July '93?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: I have one more question, but if we can please switch off the sound because I will mention a name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We can go into private session. (Private session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: 1.27 p.m., to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 16th day of March, 1999, at 9.00 a.m. 23 24 25
